summary: CrowdStrike extends Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B with 5,120 BPE byte tokens and continues training on about 630k malware, adware and benign binaries, plus 3.2M synthetic compiled-C chunks explained by an LLM. It then instruction-tunes on template-generated metadata Q&A. On its own random file-level test split it reports 89-98% file-info accuracy, 71-89% label F1 and 39-69% malware-family accuracy. Three frontier models were scored on a different 400-sample subset with fuzzy matching. The subject is malware binary classification, not software development.

claims.claim: LBM is the first byte-native LLM.
claims.evidence: The related-work section itself cites byte-level models (MEGABYTE, BLT, byteGPT). The novelty is vocabulary expansion of a text LLM with byte tokens.

Table 4. The 98% is Mistral's file-info score and the 69% is Llama's family score. These are in-distribution results on a random split of company data, with no variance. Family accuracy depends on family size in training (Fig. 4).

claims.claim: Off-the-shelf models lack both accuracy and insight; domain knowledge during training is essential.
claims.evidence: Table 5 evaluates frontier models on 400 balanced samples with fuzzy matching at a 45% threshold, with family judged manually, while LBM is evaluated on the full test set. Claude Sonnet 4.5 label F1 (77%) exceeds the real-world-only Llama LBM (71%). 'Insight' is never measured. The LoRA baseline is a weak comparator. Prompts and scripts are available only 'upon request'.

claims.claim: Adding synthetic data consistently improves classification.
claims.evidence: Table 4: RW vs RW+Syn for both base models on all three classification tasks. Opcode outlier detection stays near chance (27-41%), and the caption calls it 'choose-one-of-four' (25% chance) although §5.2 describes five opcodes.

claims.claim: Deployed to a limited number of analysts.
claims.evidence: No usage, feedback or outcome data is reported.

patterns.note: Domain knowledge is injected through fine-tuning data (templated analyst metadata), not supplied to an agent as runtime context. There is no comparison with runtime context.
Internal deployment is mentioned with no field results.

methodology.sample: 631,759 files (505k train / 126k test) and 3.16M synthetic chunks from 44 open-source C projects.
methodology.baselines: Base models, a LoRA fine-tune, and three frontier models (Nemotron 3 Super, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Llama-4 Maverick) on a different 400-sample subset.
methodology.models: Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2 with byte-vocabulary expansion.
methodology.ablations: Real-world vs real-world plus synthetic data; tokenizer training mix.
methodology.contamination_controls: Random file-level split. Near-duplicate malware variants across the split are not controlled.
methodology.languages: Binaries (PE/ELF/MachO); synthetic data compiled from C.

standards.artifacts: None released. Proprietary data and model; evaluation scripts on request.

biases.detail: Claims 'first byte-native LLM' while citing prior byte-level LLMs.
Baselines and LBM are scored on different samples with different matching (fuzzy vs exact), and label results mix F1 with weighted accuracy.
Frontier models receive raw bytes as text with no disassembly tooling, and the PEFT baseline is a minimal LoRA.
A random split of malware families likely leaks near-identical variants into the test set.
The vendor's own system is evaluated on the vendor's own data and metrics.
Malware analysis, not software development with LLMs or agents.

coi.vendor_products_evaluated: LBM, CrowdStrike's own system (presented at its Fal.Con conference), compared favorably against competitors' models.
coi.detail: The vendor evaluates its own product favorably on closed data with no independent replication.

verdict_reason: Off-topic (malware classification). It also has high COI, mismatched baseline evaluation, a novelty claim contradicted by its own related work, and nothing released.
applicability: No transfer to the team's discovery or onboarding harness. The appendix analyst survey lists generic onboarding wishes (an at-a-glance summary, pointers to the sections worth reading, a single Q&A assistant), but none are evaluated.
